topic: Reactions of alkenes and alcohols (chemistry only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: What is the general formula for the homologous series of alkenes?
items.correct: CₙH₂ₙ — twice as many hydrogen atoms as carbon atoms
items.misconception: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — two hydrogen atoms more than twice the carbon
items.why: The alkanes are met first and their formula is drilled hard, so CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ becomes the formula reached for whenever a hydrocarbon series is named. The two series differ. Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and alkenes are CₙH₂ₙ. Checking a known member settles it: propene is C₃H₆, which is 2 × 3 hydrogen atoms, not 2 × 3 + 2.
items.random_wrong: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ — two hydrogen atoms fewer than twice the carbons

items.q: Which of these is a correct description of an alkene?
items.correct: A hydrocarbon containing a carbon–carbon double bond
items.misconception: A hydrocarbon in which every carbon bond is a single bond
items.why: The alkanes are met first and their formula is drilled hard, so CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ becomes the formula reached for whenever a hydrocarbon series is named. The two series differ. Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and alkenes are CₙH₂ₙ. Checking a known member settles it: propene is C₃H₆, which is 2 × 3 hydrogen atoms, not 2 × 3 + 2.
items.random_wrong: A compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms

items.q: Propane has the formula C₃H₈. What is the formula of propene?
items.correct: C₃H₆, two hydrogen atoms fewer than propane
items.misconception: C₃H₄, which is four hydrogen atoms fewer than propane
items.why: In everyday use 'saturated' means soaked or full, so students expect the unsaturated molecule to take on extra hydrogen rather than to have less of it. The specification states it directly: alkene molecules are unsaturated because they contain two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.
items.random_wrong: C₃H₈, exactly the same formula as propane has

items.q: Why is propene described as unsaturated?
items.correct: It has two hydrogen atoms fewer than propane does
items.misconception: It has four hydrogen atoms fewer than propane does
items.why: In everyday use 'saturated' means soaked or full, so students expect the unsaturated molecule to take on extra hydrogen rather than to have less of it. The specification states it directly: alkene molecules are unsaturated because they contain two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.
items.random_wrong: Every bond between its carbon atoms is a single bond

items.q: Which list gives the first four members of the homologous series of alkenes?
items.correct: Ethene, propene, butene and pentene
items.misconception: Methene, ethene, propene and pentene
items.why: The alkanes begin with methane, so students expect every homologous series to start at one carbon atom and pattern-match the prefixes. A carbon-carbon double bond needs two carbon atoms, so the alkenes begin at ethene. The four named members are ethene, propene, butene and pentene.
items.random_wrong: Ethene, ethane, butene and butane

items.q: What does the molecular formula C₃H₆ tell you about a propene molecule?
items.correct: The number of atoms of each element in the molecule
items.misconception: Where the double bond lies and how the atoms join
items.why: Both forms describe the same molecule, so students conclude they say the same thing and treat the drawing as decoration. The written forms count or group the atoms; the displayed formula shows the bonds, so a double bond or an O–H bond can be seen directly.
items.random_wrong: Only the ratio of carbon to hydrogen atoms present

items.q: Which of these formulae fits the general formula CₙH₂ₙ?
items.correct: C₃H₆
items.misconception: C₄H₁₀
items.why: The alkanes are met first and their formula is drilled hard, so CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ becomes the formula reached for whenever a hydrocarbon series is named. The two series differ. Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and alkenes are CₙH₂ₙ. Checking a known member settles it: propene is C₃H₆, which is 2 × 3 hydrogen atoms, not 2 × 3 + 2.
items.random_wrong: C₂H₅OH

items.q: Propene can also be drawn as a fully displayed formula. What does that show that C₃H₆ does not?
items.correct: Every atom and every bond, including the double bond
items.misconception: Nothing new; the same information is drawn out
items.why: Both forms describe the same molecule, so students conclude they say the same thing and treat the drawing as decoration. The written forms count or group the atoms; the displayed formula shows the bonds, so a double bond or an O–H bond can be seen directly.
items.random_wrong: Only how many atoms of each element are present

items.q: What is the functional group of the alkenes?
items.correct: The carbon–carbon double bond, C=C
items.misconception: The –OH group found in alcohols
items.why: Alcohols are taught in the same topic as alkanes and alkenes and their names look similar, so the oxygen atom is overlooked. A hydrocarbon contains only hydrogen and carbon. Ethanol is CH₃CH₂OH, so it holds an oxygen atom and cannot be a hydrocarbon.
items.random_wrong: The –COOH group of the acids

items.q: Ethene, propene and butene all decolourise bromine water. What best explains this?
items.correct: They share a functional group, so they react alike
items.misconception: Each one has its own reaction and the likeness is chance
items.why: Reactions are often met one equation at a time, so the pattern behind them is missed and chemistry looks like a list to memorise. It is the generality of reactions of functional groups that determines the reactions of organic compounds; every member of a series reacts in the same ways.
items.random_wrong: They all contain the same number of carbon atoms

items.q: How do alkenes tend to burn in air?
items.correct: With smoky flames, because combustion is incomplete
items.misconception: They combine with the nitrogen of the air as well as the oxygen
items.why: The Bunsen burner burning methane with a clean blue flame is the image students carry, and it is applied to every hydrocarbon. Alkenes have a higher proportion of carbon, so in air the oxygen supply is not enough to burn all of it. Combustion is incomplete and the flame is smoky.
items.random_wrong: They do not burn at all, as the double bond is stable

items.q: Ethene is burned in plenty of air. What are the products of complete combustion?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide and water
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide and soot
items.why: The hydrogen atoms in the formula are tracked as though they leave unchanged, and incomplete combustion is applied whatever the air supply. In complete combustion every carbon atom ends up in CO₂ and every hydrogen atom in H₂O: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen

items.q: Hydrogen adds to ethene. What happens to the carbon–carbon double bond?
items.correct: It becomes a single carbon–carbon bond
items.misconception: It stays a double bond in the product
items.why: The extra atoms are pictured as being tacked onto the ends of the molecule, leaving the middle untouched. The atoms add across the double bond itself, so in the product the two carbon atoms are joined by a single bond.
items.random_wrong: It breaks and the molecule splits into two

items.q: Which set of substances react with alkenes by addition across the double bond?
items.correct: Hydrogen, water and the halogens
items.misconception: Oxygen, carbon dioxide and nitrogen
items.why: The Bunsen burner burning methane with a clean blue flame is the image students carry, and it is applied to every hydrocarbon. Alkenes have a higher proportion of carbon, so in air the oxygen supply is not enough to burn all of it. Combustion is incomplete and the flame is smoky.
items.random_wrong: Oxygen, sodium and the halogens

items.q: What conditions are used for the addition of hydrogen to an alkene?
items.correct: A nickel catalyst at about 150 °C
items.misconception: Ultraviolet light, no catalyst
items.why: Ultraviolet light is the one condition students remember from organic chemistry, so it is offered for any organic reaction. Ultraviolet light belongs to the substitution reactions of alkanes. Hydrogenation of an alkene uses a nickel catalyst at roughly 150 °C.
items.random_wrong: Steam with a catalyst at 300 °C

items.q: Ethene is reacted with steam in the presence of a catalyst. What is produced?
items.correct: Ethanol, an alcohol, CH₃CH₂OH
items.misconception: Ethane gas, an alkane, C₂H₆
items.why: Hydrogen and water both add across a C=C, so their products are mixed up, and 'steam' is read as a solvent rather than a reactant. Adding hydrogen gives the alkane; adding water gives the alcohol. Ethene with steam and a catalyst gives ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH.
items.random_wrong: Ethanoic acid, an acid, CH₃COOH

items.q: Bromine water is shaken with ethene. What is seen, and what is formed?
items.correct: The orange colour goes and C₂H₄Br₂ forms
items.misconception: The orange colour goes as C₂H₃Br and HBr form
items.why: Substitution is met first, with alkanes and halogens in ultraviolet light, and the pattern is carried over to the alkenes. Alkanes substitute, alkenes add. The double bond opens and both halogen atoms join the molecule, so nothing is left over.
items.random_wrong: The orange colour stays, as ethene is saturated

items.q: Ethene reacts with chlorine. Which describes the product?
items.correct: C₂H₄Cl₂, one chlorine atom on each carbon atom
items.misconception: C₂H₃Cl, with a hydrogen atom replaced by chlorine
items.why: Substitution is met first, with alkanes and halogens in ultraviolet light, and the pattern is carried over to the alkenes. Alkanes substitute, alkenes add. The double bond opens and both halogen atoms join the molecule, so nothing is left over.
items.random_wrong: C₂H₄ and Cl₂ are unchanged, as there is no reaction

items.q: Propene reacts with hydrogen. How many hydrogen atoms are in the displayed formula of the product?
items.correct: Eight, since the product is propane, C₃H₈
items.misconception: Six, as propene already has six of them
items.why: Students reason that two bonds take more energy to break than one, and conclude the molecule must be harder to react. Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes. The double bond is a site where atoms can add on, which is why bromine water is decolourised by an alkene but not by an alkane.
items.random_wrong: Seven, one hydrogen atom having added on

items.q: Which functional group is found in every alcohol?
items.correct: The hydroxyl group, –OH
items.misconception: The carboxyl group, –COOH
items.why: The two endings differ by very little in print and the stems are identical, so the families blur together. The ending names the functional group. Propanol contains –OH; propanoic acid contains –COOH and gives an acidic solution.
items.random_wrong: A carbon–carbon double bond

items.q: Which list gives the first four members of the homologous series of alcohols?
items.correct: Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol
items.misconception: Methanol, ethanol, propanol and pentanol
items.why: The alkanes begin with methane, so students expect every homologous series to start at one carbon atom and pattern-match the prefixes. A carbon-carbon double bond needs two carbon atoms, so the alkenes begin at ethene. The four named members are ethene, propene, butene and pentene.
items.random_wrong: Ethanol, propanol, butanol, pentanol

items.q: Ethanol can be represented as CH₃CH₂OH. What does this form show?
items.correct: The –OH group and how the carbon atoms are grouped
items.misconception: Only the total number of atoms of each element
items.why: Empirical formulae and molecular formulae are met together, and equation writing is treated as translation rather than as balancing. A molecular formula gives real numbers, not a ratio, and an equation is only correct when the atoms of each element balance on both sides.
items.random_wrong: Every bond in the molecule, drawn in full

items.q: A displayed formula of ethanol is drawn instead of writing CH₃CH₂OH. What does the drawing add?
items.correct: It shows every bond, including the O–H bond
items.misconception: It shows nothing new about the ethanol molecule
items.why: Both forms describe the same molecule, so students conclude they say the same thing and treat the drawing as decoration. The written forms count or group the atoms; the displayed formula shows the bonds, so a double bond or an O–H bond can be seen directly.
items.random_wrong: It shows how many molecules are in the sample

items.q: A small piece of sodium is added to ethanol. What is observed?
items.correct: It fizzes steadily and hydrogen gas is given off
items.misconception: It fizzes gently and oxygen is given off
items.why: Students look for the released gas among the atoms they can see, and the O of the –OH group is the obvious candidate. It is the hydrogen of the –OH group that is displaced by sodium, so hydrogen gas fizzes off, just as when sodium reacts with water.
items.random_wrong: Nothing happens; sodium reacts only with water

items.q: Ethanol burns completely in air. What are the products?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide and water
items.misconception: Carbon monoxide and water
items.why: The hydrogen atoms in the formula are tracked as though they leave unchanged, and incomplete combustion is applied whatever the air supply. In complete combustion every carbon atom ends up in CO₂ and every hydrogen atom in H₂O: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen

items.q: Which equation correctly represents the complete combustion of ethanol?
items.correct: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
items.misconception: C₂H₅OH + 2O₂ → 2CO₂ + H₂O
items.why: Empirical formulae and molecular formulae are met together, and equation writing is treated as translation rather than as balancing. A molecular formula gives real numbers, not a ratio, and an equation is only correct when the atoms of each element balance on both sides.
items.random_wrong: C₂H₅OH + O₂ → 2CO₂ + H₂O

items.q: What happens when ethanol is added to water?
items.correct: It dissolves fully, giving a neutral solution
items.misconception: It dissolves and the solution has a pH below 7
items.why: The names ethanol and ethanoic acid are almost the same, and both molecules contain an O–H, so their solutions are expected to behave alike. Alcohols dissolve to give neutral solutions. Only after oxidation, when the carboxyl group has formed, is the solution acidic.
items.random_wrong: It floats as a layer and does not mix at all

items.q: Ethanol is warmed with an oxidising agent. What is formed?
items.correct: Ethanoic acid, which is a carboxylic acid
items.misconception: Ethene, formed by the loss of a water molecule
items.why: Several reactions of ethanol are met close together, and 'oxidising agent' is read as another way of saying burning, or confused with dehydration. Oxidation of an alcohol gives the carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms, so ethanol gives ethanoic acid.
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide and water, as when it burns

items.q: Which statement gives main uses of the first four alcohols?
items.correct: They are used as fuels and as solvents
items.misconception: They are used only for alcoholic drinks
items.why: The word alcohol has an everyday meaning that crowds out the chemistry. Methanol and ethanol burn cleanly and are used as fuels, and alcohols dissolve substances that water will not, so they are widely used as solvents.
items.random_wrong: They are drunk in beverages and have no other use

items.q: How are aqueous solutions of ethanol produced from sugar?
items.correct: The sugar solution is fermented using yeast
items.misconception: The sugar solution is fermented at about 100 °C
items.why: Rate work teaches that heating speeds reactions up, and the rule is applied without asking what heat does to the yeast. Yeast is a living organism and its enzymes are denatured by heat, so fermentation is carried out warm, at roughly 30 °C, not hot.
items.random_wrong: The sugar is reacted with steam and a catalyst

items.q: Which conditions are used for the fermentation of sugar using yeast?
items.correct: About 30 °C, in solution, with air kept out
items.misconception: About 100 °C, in solution, with air kept out
items.why: Rate work teaches that heating speeds reactions up, and the rule is applied without asking what heat does to the yeast. Yeast is a living organism and its enzymes are denatured by heat, so fermentation is carried out warm, at roughly 30 °C, not hot.
items.random_wrong: About 30 °C, in solution, with air bubbled in

items.q: Which of these formulae is that of an alcohol?
items.correct: CH₃CH₂OH
items.misconception: CH₃COOH
items.why: Students scan for the letters OH rather than reading the whole functional group. In a carboxylic acid the O–H sits on a carbon that is also double bonded to oxygen. That whole –COOH group, not the O–H alone, is the functional group.
items.random_wrong: C₃H₆

items.q: Which functional group do carboxylic acids contain?
items.correct: The carboxyl group, –COOH
items.misconception: The hydroxyl group, –OH
items.why: The two endings differ by very little in print and the stems are identical, so the families blur together. The ending names the functional group. Propanol contains –OH; propanoic acid contains –COOH and gives an acidic solution.
items.random_wrong: A carbon–carbon double bond

items.q: Which list gives the first four members of the homologous series of carboxylic acids?
items.correct: Methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid
items.misconception: Ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic, pentanoic acid
items.why: The alkanes begin with methane, so students expect every homologous series to start at one carbon atom and pattern-match the prefixes. A carbon-carbon double bond needs two carbon atoms, so the alkenes begin at ethene. The four named members are ethene, propene, butene and pentene.
items.random_wrong: Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol

items.q: Ethanoic acid can be represented as CH₃COOH. What does this form show?
items.correct: A –COOH group joined to a CH₃ group
items.misconception: An –OH group on a chain of two carbons
items.why: Students scan for the letters OH rather than reading the whole functional group. In a carboxylic acid the O–H sits on a carbon that is also double bonded to oxygen. That whole –COOH group, not the O–H alone, is the functional group.
items.random_wrong: Every bond of the acid, drawn out

items.q: Ethanoic acid is added to sodium carbonate. What happens?
items.correct: It fizzes and carbon dioxide gas is given off
items.misconception: It fizzes as vigorously as dilute hydrochloric acid does
items.why: Two fizzing reactions are learned close together and the gases are swapped. Acid with a metal gives hydrogen; acid with a carbonate gives carbon dioxide, which turns limewater cloudy.
items.random_wrong: There is no reaction, since it is only a weak acid

items.q: What happens when ethanoic acid dissolves in water?
items.correct: An acidic solution forms, with a pH below 7
items.misconception: A neutral solution forms, as with ethanol
items.why: In everyday speech weak and dilute mean much the same, and 'weak' sounds like 'unable'. Strength is about the fraction of molecules that ionise; concentration is about how much acid is dissolved. A weak acid still reacts, for instance with carbonates.
items.random_wrong: It does not dissolve, being an organic liquid

items.q: Ethanoic acid is warmed with ethanol and an acid catalyst. What is formed?
items.correct: Ethyl ethanoate, an ester, together with water
items.misconception: A salt and water only, as in neutralisation
items.why: 'Acid plus something gives a salt and water' is a strong rule from acid chemistry, and the alcohol is treated as if it were an alkali. An alcohol is not an alkali. The acid and the alcohol join to make an ester: ethanoic acid with ethanol gives ethyl ethanoate.
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide and water, as with a carbonate

items.q: Why is ethanoic acid described as a weak acid?
items.correct: Only some of its molecules ionise in solution
items.misconception: All of its molecules ionise in aqueous solution
items.why: Strong acids are met first and their full ionisation is taken as what 'acid' means. A strong acid is completely ionised in solution; a weak acid, such as a carboxylic acid, is only partially ionised.
items.random_wrong: Its solutions are dilute rather than concentrated

items.q: Solutions of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid have the same concentration. How do their pH values compare?
items.correct: Ethanoic acid has the higher pH of the two
items.misconception: Ethanoic acid has the lower pH of the two
items.why: Equal concentrations are assumed to mean equal numbers of H+ ions, and the difference between strength and concentration is not applied. Only some ethanoic acid molecules ionise, so its solution has fewer H+ ions and a higher pH than hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.
items.random_wrong: Both have the same pH, as both are acids

items.q: Which of these formulae is that of a carboxylic acid?
items.correct: CH₃CH₂COOH
items.misconception: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH
items.why: The two endings differ by very little in print and the stems are identical, so the families blur together. The ending names the functional group. Propanol contains –OH; propanoic acid contains –COOH and gives an acidic solution.
items.random_wrong: CH₃CH₂OH

items.q: What does a molecular formula such as C₃H₆ show?
items.correct: How many atoms of each element are in one molecule.
items.misconception: A displayed or structural formula is thought to tell you how the molecules are arranged, or how many molecules there are, in a bulk sample — confusing one molecule's structure with the bulk.
items.why: Formulae and drawings are used side by side in lessons, so students stop distinguishing what each representation actually carries. C₃H₆ counts atoms only. To see the bonds, and where the C=C lies, a fully displayed formula is needed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to an alkene molecule in an addition reaction?
items.correct: Atoms add across the C=C, which becomes a single bond.
items.misconception: The molecule breaks apart at the double bond into two smaller molecules.
items.why: 'The double bond breaks' is a phrase used in class, and students take it to mean the carbon chain itself splits, as it does in cracking. Only one of the two bonds between the carbon atoms is used. The carbon chain stays whole and the double bond becomes a single carbon-carbon bond.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are alcohol solutions alkaline?
items.correct: No: the first four alcohols dissolve to give neutral solutions.
items.misconception: The –OH group makes alcohols alkaline, because alkalis contain OH.
items.why: Hydroxide ions, OH-, are met in alkalis, and the same two letters in the alcohol functional group are read as the same thing. In an alcohol the –OH is covalently bonded within the molecule and no hydroxide ions are released, so the solution is neutral.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is air needed for fermentation?
items.correct: No: fermentation is carried out with air kept out.
items.misconception: Air must be bubbled through, because yeast needs oxygen.
items.why: Respiration is remembered as needing oxygen, so oxygen is assumed to be needed here too. Fermentation is anaerobic. If air is present the ethanol is oxidised, so the vessel is kept sealed from the air.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which bonds are found in a saturated molecule?
items.correct: Single carbon-carbon bonds only.
items.misconception: Saturated and unsaturated are used the other way round, so an alkene is called saturated.
items.why: The two terms are abstract, sound similar and are introduced together, so they are easily swapped. Saturated means every carbon-carbon bond is single, as in the alkanes. Unsaturated means a C=C is present, as in the alkenes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why do alkenes burn with smoky flames?
items.correct: Because combustion is incomplete and carbon is released.
items.misconception: Because there is too much oxygen present when they burn.
items.why: Smoke is linked with something being wrong with the air supply, but the direction of the effect is guessed. A smoky flame means too little oxygen for the carbon present, so some carbon is not oxidised and appears as soot.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does sodium react with ethanol?
items.correct: Yes: it fizzes and releases hydrogen.
items.misconception: Sodium reacts only with water, so nothing happens with an alcohol.
items.why: The reaction of sodium with water is memorable and is taken to be the only reaction sodium has with an O–H containing liquid. Alcohols react with sodium in the same way as water, though more gently, giving off hydrogen gas.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do ethanol and ethanoic acid dissolve in water?
items.correct: Yes: both are soluble in water.
items.misconception: Organic liquids do not mix with water; they float as a separate layer.
items.why: Oil and water is the everyday example of an organic liquid meeting water, and it is generalised. The first four alcohols dissolve to give neutral solutions and the carboxylic acids dissolve to give acidic solutions.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many hydrogen atoms are added when hydrogen reacts with propene?
items.correct: Two, giving propane, C₃H₈.
items.misconception: One hydrogen atom is added, or two whole molecules of hydrogen are.
items.why: Students count the molecule H₂ as a single unit of one atom, or add reagent until the formula looks familiar. One molecule of H₂ supplies two atoms, one to each carbon of the double bond, so C₃H₆ becomes C₃H₈.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.7.2 Reactions of alkenes and alcohols (chemistry only)
